newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin may look abroad to try to pay wage debt.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin may look abroad to try to pay wage debt.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Friday Russia may seek foreign assistance to pay wage arrears to public sector workers, such as teachers and doctors, in the next three months, Itar-Tass news agency said.
Tass quoted Yeltsin as saying at a meeting with Russian regional leaders that additional ways must be sought to wipe out the wage debts on time, including looking abroad.
"Let's turn to leaders of foreign countries," Yeltsin added. He gave no details.
Yeltsin, 66, has made paying the backlog of wages to public sector workers and the military one of the government's main tasks in the coming months.

Tass said First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who was also present at the meeting in the Kremlin with regional leaders, had expressed coubt that it would be possible to pay the wage debts in all regions in such a short time.
"It is not a realistic task for all the regions at the same time," Tass quoted Chubais as saying.

Yeltsin responded by saying the government had recently managed to pay off pension arrears rapidly and that it was necessary now to "continue pursuing this line and under no circumstances permit any delays or let the debt accumulate."
"It is possible if we all pull together," Tass quoted him as saying. Yeltsin gave no more details of how Russia might try to raise the money.

Tass did not say how much public sector workers were owed. But wage arrears just to the armed forces, which Yeltsin has said must be paid in the next two months, total about five trillion roubles ($860 million).

The World Bank approved an $800 million loan in June to help pay pensions and cushion the social effects of reform measures, but only $300 million will be available immediately. The rest will depend on government steps towards pension reform.
Russia is also in the second year of a three-year $10 billion loan programme from the International Monetary Fund.
It received its first $700 million quarterly disbursal for 1997 in May and further disbursements will be contingent on Russia meeting agreed budget targets.
